stem: According to Mendeleev's periodic law, properties of elements are a periodic function of their _______.
solution: Mendeleev arranged elements in increasing order of their atomic masses and stated that the properties of elements are a periodic function of their atomic masses. (Later, the modern periodic law used atomic number.)

stem: The vapour content in the air is measured using a physical quantity called _______.
solution: Absolute humidity is the actual mass of water vapour present per unit volume of air, i.e. it measures the vapour content of the air.

stem: For the normal human eye, the near point is at _______ cm.
solution: The near point (least distance of distinct vision) of a normal human eye is 25 cm.

stem: The astronomical object closest to us is _______.
solution: The Moon is the natural satellite of the Earth and is the astronomical object closest to us (about 3,84,000 km away).

stem: In the Wilfley table method, the particles of gangue are separated by _______ separation method.
solution: The Wilfley table (shaking table) method is a hydraulic separation method: a stream of water carries away the lighter gangue particles while the heavier ore particles settle behind the riffles.

stem: Find the odd one out: Voltmeter, Ammeter, Thermometer, Galvanometer.
solution: Thermometer is the odd one out. Voltmeter, ammeter and galvanometer are electrical measuring instruments, whereas a thermometer measures temperature.

stem: Complete the correlation: Alkene : C \(=\) C :: Alkyne : _______.
solution: Alkyne : C \(\equiv\) C. An alkene has a carbon-carbon double bond, while an alkyne has a carbon-carbon triple bond.

stem: State true or false: The frequency of AC is 50 Hz.
solution: True. In India, the frequency of alternating current (AC) supply is 50 Hz.

stem: Name the first artificial satellite sent by Russia in space.
solution: Sputnik (Sputnik-1) was the first artificial satellite, launched by Russia (the erstwhile USSR) in 1957.

stem: Give scientific reason: The weight of an object changes from place to place though its mass is constant.
solution: The weight of an object is the force with which the Earth attracts it, given by \(W = mg\). The mass \(m\) is the amount of matter and stays constant everywhere. But the acceleration due to gravity \(g\) changes from place to place (it is greater at the poles than at the equator, and decreases with altitude and depth). Since \(g\) varies, the weight \(W = mg\) also changes from place to place even though the mass remains constant.

stem: Give scientific reason: Stars twinkle but we do not see the twinkling of planets.
solution: Stars are very far away and act as point sources of light. As starlight passes through the Earth's atmosphere, it undergoes continuous atmospheric refraction due to changing air densities, so the apparent position and brightness of the star keep fluctuating - the star appears to twinkle. Planets are much closer and act as an extended collection of a large number of point sources. The twinkling from these many points averages out (nullifies) and the total light received remains almost steady, so planets do not appear to twinkle.

stem: Give scientific reason: Elements belonging to the same group have the same valency.
solution: Elements in the same group of the modern periodic table have the same number of valence electrons (electrons in the outermost shell). Since valency is determined by the number of valence electrons (the electrons that participate in bonding), elements of the same group show the same valency. For example, all Group 1 (alkali metals) have 1 valence electron and valency 1.

stem: How much heat energy is necessary to raise the temperature of 5 kg of water from \(20^\circ C\) to \(100^\circ C\)? (specific heat of water \(= 4200 \ \mathrm{J/kg\,^\circ C}\))
solution:
Given: \(m = 5 \ \mathrm{kg}\), \(\Delta T = 100 - 20 = 80^\circ C\), \(c = 4200 \ \mathrm{J/kg\,^\circ C}\).
Heat required \(Q = mc\,\Delta T = 5 \times 4200 \times 80 = 16{,}80{,}000 \ \mathrm{J} = 1680 \ \mathrm{kJ}\).
(Equivalently, using \(c = 1 \ \mathrm{kcal/kg\,^\circ C}\): \(Q = 5 \times 1 \times 80 = 400 \ \mathrm{kcal}\).)

stem: Observe the given figure of Fleming's Right Hand Rule (the thumb shows the motion of a conductor) and write the labels of A and B correctly.
solution:
By Fleming's Right Hand Rule, when the thumb, forefinger and middle finger of the right hand are held mutually perpendicular: the thumb shows the direction of motion of the conductor, A (forefinger) shows the direction of the magnetic field, and B (middle finger) shows the direction of the induced current.
A = Direction of magnetic field
B = Direction of induced current
figureNote: Fleming's Right Hand Rule: an outstretched right hand with the thumb pointing up (labelled 'Motion of a conductor') and two empty label boxes A and B for the forefinger and middle finger directions. Page 1.

stem:
Observe the given graph of the volume of 1 kg of water versus temperature and answer:
a. Name the process represented in the figure.
b. At what temperature does this process take place?
solution:
a. The graph represents the anomalous (abnormal) expansion of water - as water is cooled its volume decreases up to \(4^\circ C\), then on cooling further below \(4^\circ C\) its volume increases again.
b. The volume of water is minimum (density is maximum) at \(4^\circ C\); i.e. the anomalous behaviour is centred at \(4^\circ C\).
figureNote: Graph of 'Volume of 1 kg water' (y-axis, 0.00-0.30) versus 'Temperature °C' (x-axis, 0-10) showing a U-shaped curve with minimum volume at 4°C. Page 2.

stem:
Complete the given chemical reaction and name the type of reaction:
\(\mathrm{CuSO_4\,(aq) + Fe\,(s) \rightarrow \underline{\qquad} + \underline{\qquad}}\)
solution:
\(\mathrm{CuSO_4\,(aq) + Fe\,(s) \rightarrow FeSO_4\,(aq) + Cu\,(s)}\)
Type of reaction: Displacement reaction (a single displacement reaction) - iron, being more reactive than copper, displaces copper from copper sulphate solution.

stem: Write a short note on Alloying.
solution: Alloying is the process of mixing a metal with one or more other metals or non-metals in a definite proportion (in the molten state) to obtain a homogeneous mixture called an alloy. It is done to improve the properties of the metal - increasing hardness and strength, lowering the melting point, and increasing resistance to corrosion. For example, steel is an alloy of iron and carbon; brass is an alloy of copper and zinc; bronze is an alloy of copper and tin; and solder is an alloy of lead and tin.

subtopic: Electronic Configuration and Position in Periodic Table
stem:
An element has its electronic configuration as 2, 8, 2. Now answer the following:
a. What is the atomic number of this element?
b. What is the group of this element?
c. To which period does this element belong?
solution:
a. Atomic number = total number of electrons = 2 + 8 + 2 = 12 (the element is Magnesium).
b. The outermost shell has 2 electrons, so the element belongs to Group 2 (IIA).
c. There are 3 occupied shells, so the element belongs to Period 3.

stem: Observe the given figure showing the orbit of a planet moving around the Sun and write the three laws related to it.
solution:
The three Kepler's laws of planetary motion are:
1. Law of orbits: The orbit of a planet is an ellipse with the Sun at one of its foci.
2. Law of areas: The line joining a planet and the Sun sweeps out equal areas in equal intervals of time (so the areal velocity of a planet is constant).
3. Law of periods: The square of the period of revolution of a planet around the Sun is directly proportional to the cube of the mean distance of the planet from the Sun, i.e. \(T^2 \propto r^3\).
figureNote: Diagram of an elliptical orbit with the Sun (S) at a focus and a planet at position A; three shaded equal-area sectors (labelled 1, 2, 3) between points A-B, C-D and E-F illustrating Kepler's law of areas. Titled 'The orbit of a planet moving around the Sun'. Page 2.

stem:
Read the given passage and answer:
The home electrical connection consists of 'live', 'neutral' and 'earth' wires. The 'live' and the 'neutral' wires have a potential difference of 220 V. The 'earth' is connected to ground. Due to a fault in the equipment, or if the plastic coating on the 'live' and 'neutral' wires gives way and the two wires come in contact, a large current flows producing heat, and any inflammable material around can catch fire. Therefore a fuse wire is used as a precautionary measure.
a. Name the two wires having a potential difference of 220 V.
b. What is a short circuit?
c. Write the function of a fuse.
solution:
a. The 'live' wire and the 'neutral' wire have a potential difference of 220 V.
b. A short circuit occurs when the live and neutral wires come in direct contact (their insulation gives way), so that the resistance of the circuit becomes almost zero and a very large current flows through it, producing excessive heat.
c. A fuse is a safety device made of a wire of low melting point. When the current in the circuit exceeds a safe limit (as during a short circuit or overloading), the fuse wire heats up, melts and breaks the circuit, thus stopping the current flow and preventing damage or fire.

stem:
Observe the given figure (a ray AC travelling from air into a glass block, refracting along CB, with angle of incidence i and angle of refraction r about the normal N) and answer:
a. Name the process represented by the figure.
b. State the two laws related to the process.
solution:
a. The process is refraction of light - the bending of a ray of light as it passes obliquely from one transparent medium (air) into another (glass).
b. The two laws of refraction (Snell's laws) are:
1. The incident ray, the refracted ray and the normal to the surface at the point of incidence all lie in the same plane.
2. For a given pair of media, the ratio of the sine of the angle of incidence to the sine of the angle of refraction is a constant, equal to the refractive index of the second medium with respect to the first: \(\dfrac{\sin i}{\sin r} = \text{constant} \ (n)\).
figureNote: Ray diagram: incident ray AC in Air striking a glass surface at C, normal N drawn, angle of incidence i, refracted ray CB bending towards the normal inside the Glass block with angle of refraction r (points C, D, B). Page 2.

stem: What is an artificial satellite? Name any two types of artificial satellite and state their functions.
solution:
An artificial satellite is a man-made object that is deliberately placed into an orbit around the Earth (or another celestial body) to perform a specific task.
Two types and their functions:
1. Communication satellite - used for relaying television, radio, telephone and internet signals over long distances.
2. Weather (meteorological) satellite - used to observe and forecast the weather by monitoring clouds, storms and atmospheric conditions.
(Other examples: navigational satellites - for GPS/position finding; Earth-observation/remote-sensing satellites - for surveying natural resources.)

Answer the following:
a. Define hydrocarbons.
b. Name the types of hydrocarbons.
c. Name two carbon compounds used in day-to-day life.
solution:
a. Hydrocarbons are organic compounds made up of only two elements, carbon and hydrogen.
b. Types of hydrocarbons: (i) Saturated hydrocarbons (alkanes - only single bonds) and (ii) Unsaturated hydrocarbons (alkenes with a double bond and alkynes with a triple bond).
c. Two carbon compounds used in day-to-day life: ethanol (used in alcoholic beverages/sanitizers) and acetic acid (vinegar). (Other acceptable examples: methane/LPG as fuel, glucose, etc.)

Observe the given figure of the reactivity series of metals and answer:
a. Name two metals which react with water.
b. Name two moderately reactive metals.
c. Name the most highly reactive metal and the most less reactive metal.
solution:
a. Two metals which react with water (highly reactive metals): Potassium and Sodium (also Lithium, Calcium).
b. Two moderately reactive metals: Zinc and Iron (also Magnesium, Aluminium, Tin, Lead).
c. The most highly reactive metal is Potassium (top of the series) and the most less (least) reactive metal is Gold (bottom of the series).

subtopic: Human Eye - Structure and Image Formation
stem:
Draw a scientifically correct labelled diagram of a human eye and answer the questions based on it:
a. Name the type of lens in the human eye.
b. Name the screen at which the maximum amount of incident light is refracted.
c. State the nature of the image formed of the object on the screen inside the eye.
solution:
(Draw a labelled diagram of the human eye showing cornea, aqueous humour, iris, pupil, eye lens (ciliary muscles), vitreous humour, retina, optic nerve and blind spot.)
a. The human eye lens is a convex lens (a biconvex, flexible lens).
b. Maximum refraction of the incident light takes place at the cornea (the outer transparent front surface of the eye).
c. The image formed on the retina (the screen inside the eye) is real, inverted and diminished (smaller than the object).

stem:
Observe the picture of rusting of iron (a water drop on an iron surface, with collected rust \(\mathrm{Fe_2O_3\cdot H_2O}\), \(\mathrm{O_2}\), \(\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}\) ions, electrons flowing, an anode region and a cathode region) and answer:
a. What is a rust?
b. Write the chemical formula of rust.
c. Write the reaction of oxidation of iron at the anode.
d. Write the reaction (reduction) that occurs at the cathode.
e. What is corrosion?
solution:
a. Rust is the brownish-red flaky layer of hydrated iron(III) oxide that forms on the surface of iron when it is exposed to moist air (oxygen and water).
b. Chemical formula of rust: \(\mathrm{Fe_2O_3\cdot xH_2O}\) (hydrated ferric oxide).
c. Oxidation of iron at the anode: \(\mathrm{Fe \rightarrow Fe^{2+} + 2e^{-}}\).
d. Reaction at the cathode (reduction of oxygen): \(\mathrm{O_2 + 4H^{+} + 4e^{-} \rightarrow 2H_2O}\).
e. Corrosion is the slow, gradual eating away (deterioration) of the surface of a metal due to its reaction with air, moisture, acids or other substances in its surroundings (e.g. rusting of iron, green coating on copper, black coating on silver).
figureNote: Electrochemical rusting diagram: a water drop on an iron surface; at the edge (cathode) \(\mathrm{O_2 + 4H^+ + 4e^- \rightarrow 2H_2O}\) with collected rust \(\mathrm{Fe_2O_3\cdot H_2O}\); at the anode iron dissolves \(\mathrm{Fe \rightarrow Fe^{2+} + 2e^-}\); electrons flow through the iron from anode to cathode. Page 3.
